summary: In this episode, the hosts discuss the Second Coming of Christ, challenging common misconceptions and exploring the biblical and theological foundations for this event. They argue that the Second Coming is not a 'cope' invented by early Christians to explain Jesus' failure to establish the Messianic kingdom, but rather a concept deeply rooted in the Old Testament and the New Testament's interpretation of it. They emphasize that Christ's ascension did not mean His absence; rather, He is present through the Holy Spirit and actively ruling in the midst of His enemies. The episode also connects the Second Coming to the Transfiguration, the resurrection of the dead, and the transformation of the entire cosmos, highlighting the positive, hopeful aspects of this eschatological event.

entities.title: Moses
entities.summary: Old Testament prophet who appears at the Transfiguration, representing the Law.

entities.title: Elijah
entities.summary: Old Testament prophet who appears at the Transfiguration, representing the Prophets.

entities.title: John the Baptist
entities.summary: The forerunner of Christ, who came in the spirit of Elijah, but is not Elijah reincarnated.

entities.title: Enoch
entities.summary: Old Testament figure who did not die, and is sometimes identified as one of the two witnesses in Revelation.

entities.title: David
entities.summary: King of Israel, ancestor of the Messiah, and author of many Psalms.

entities.title: St. Paul
entities.summary: Apostle who wrote many New Testament letters, using terms like 'parousia' and 'first fruits'.

entities.title: St. John
entities.summary: Apostle and author of the Gospel of John, Revelation, and epistles.

entities.title: St. Gregory Palamas
entities.summary: Orthodox theologian who wrote about the vision of uncreated light and the divine energies.

entities.title: Theotokos
entities.summary: The Virgin Mary, Mother of God, whose conception of Christ is paralleled to the Eucharist.

concepts.title: Second Coming of Christ
concepts.summary: The anticipated return of Christ at the end of the age, which is not a mere 'second coming' but a unique event of His appearing in glory to judge and transform creation.

concepts.title: Parousia
concepts.summary: A Greek term used in the New Testament for Christ's coming, meaning 'being present in person' or 'arrival', emphasizing that Christ is not absent but will be present in a new way.

concepts.title: Epiphany (Epiphaneia)
concepts.summary: A Greek term meaning 'appearing' or 'manifestation', used in the New Testament to describe Christ's glorious appearing, drawing on Old Testament theophanies.

concepts.title: Apocalypse (Apokalypsis)
concepts.summary: A Greek term meaning 'revelation' or 'unveiling', used to describe Christ's revealing at the end of days, connecting to prophetic visions in the Old Testament.

concepts.title: Ascension
concepts.summary: The event where Christ was taken up into heaven, not as a departure but as His enthronement at the right hand of God, signifying His ongoing presence and rule.

concepts.title: Transfiguration
concepts.summary: The event where Christ revealed His divine glory to Peter, James, and John, serving as a glimpse of the resurrection and the world to come.

concepts.title: First Fruits
concepts.summary: An agricultural metaphor used by St. Paul to describe Christ's resurrection as the guarantee of the future resurrection of believers and the transformation of creation.

concepts.title: Spiritual Body
concepts.summary: The resurrected body that is permeated by the Holy Spirit, not a non-physical or ephemeral body, but a transformed physical body.

concepts.title: Divine Council
concepts.summary: The heavenly assembly of divine beings, over which Christ rules, as depicted in the Transfiguration and Psalm 82.

claims.text: The Second Coming is not a 'cope' invented by early Christians to explain Jesus' failure to establish the kingdom; it is rooted in Old Testament expectations.
Christ's ascension did not mean His absence; He is present through the Holy Spirit and actively ruling in the midst of His enemies.
The Greek term 'parousia' means 'being present in person', used for the visit of an emperor, and is applied to Christ's coming.
The Transfiguration is a glimpse of the resurrected Christ and the world to come, showing the kingdom of God.
Christ's resurrection is the 'first fruits' guaranteeing the future resurrection of believers and the transformation of creation.
The 'spiritual body' in the resurrection is not ephemeral but a body permeated by the Holy Spirit.
Christ is currently ruling in the midst of His enemies, as described in Psalm 110, and this period is not a pause but part of His messianic work.
John the Baptist came in the spirit of Elijah, but he is not Elijah reincarnated; the two witnesses in Revelation may be Enoch and Elijah, but not literally.
